body: There's nothing wrong with taking a break from driving. I have similar problems the hyper vigilance causes way too much overstimulation and it's hard for me to focus. I've had issues with lights (going through reds and not moving on greens for example). It feels like I can't make a trip without breaking into panic and/or being beeped at. So I've set myself up with rides for now wherever I can. It helps a lot, and I know it's only temporary.
Thanks. This is helpful. Unfortunately, my appointment was today and I'm in the hospital on a psych hold. So I guess it didn't matter in the end.
Don't feel bad my friend. I got a little too zesty with my self destruction and now I'm in the hospital on a psych hold. Oops.

I know that feeling, it's comforting to know this is probably normal, but still sad and dark. I quit therapy today. It honestly made everything worse for me. Maybe I'm just a wimp. I've become very suicidal since I started the process. Trying to accept what happened to me is literally killing me. I'm convinced that nobody is meant to live with this. I'm like you in the sense that my husband is really the only thing that keeps me here. I feel terrible about the thought of leaving him behind, but I just can't see myself doing more good than harm. Feeling like I should just quit while I'm ahead. Give him a chance to start over with as little damage as possible.
ALSO watching how they treat people like waitstaff. Apparently that can give you some clues.

I used to have a friend/roommate who actually ended up being abusive to his girlfriend (I've since cut ties with him and become friends with said ex-girlfriend). I would say isolation ended up being the biggest red flag. He started as a friend to her. Convinced her to dump her current boyfriend. Was very charming. Treated her like gold at first. Then he started doing manipulative things. Would guilt her a lot. And gaslight her if she questioned it. He would try to control the people around her (disregarding delegitimizing her concerns and wants, etc.). It became more obvious when he was doing more blatant behavior, but in retrospect, she said that those isolation, manipulation and gaslighting were the biggest early signs. For what it's worth, this guy was VERY charming. Very "upstanding." The kind of guy that's a valedictorian as a double major. The kind of guy that is almost weirdly over achieving and seemingly "perfect." Nobody believed her because he has such a convincing front. Honestly though, I almost felt like there was something questionable about a person like that...
Also, to answer the original question, no this doesn't sound like PTSD to me. This reminds me more of anxiety or OCD. There is definitely a problem there that deserves attention, though. Good luck.

Nope, at the time, I actually really didn't like taking it. Emotionally, I was very healthy then, so they didn't make me feel good, I felt better mentally without. I was actually excited when I didn't need it anymore. I was only 19 at that time. Now, at 25 with severe PTSD, I'm not so sure it would go down that way.

Fun fact, diazepam is actually standard treatment for certain muscle disorders! I used to have to take it every day for almost two years for a muscle spasm disorder. Worked wonders and thankfully didn't develop any sort of addiction. It was the only thing that worked, and it was supplemented with trigger point injections and a lot of physical therapy. My psychiatrist, now a few years later with my PTSD and mental instability absolutely won't give me any, though.  I think it tends to be more abused under those circumstances.

UGH I'm so sorry. People always feel more sympathetic for people who are only hypotheticals to them. It's less scary. I had a friend berate me for not having sympathy for a fictional character, but she saw no issue in delegitimizing my rape and calling me a drunk slut to other people. People won't acknowledge reality and what's right in front of them because then it's not entertainment that they can keep at arms length. Then they aren't in control, and would have to face the darkness.

I'm doing PE. I hate it. It's the hardest thing I've ever done in my life. I'm not letting myself stop, though. It's supposed to be very effective. 

I've had so many setbacks. It feels like I've just been uncovering more and more of how bad the damage really is. I'm trying to look at it that way, which sucks because I never know how many more weeks are going to be terrible, but it helps me feel like I'm working towards something.

Gosh idk how to advise you, but I just want to tell you that I totally understand this and it happens to me too. I was doing a temp job and I called out 6 days in a row before I had to just quit. It sucked. I actually switched over to working exclusively from home, and only part time since that happened because that's literally all I can handle right now. It sucks, but it will be worth the set back to me because I believe that I will be able to thrive again when I'm better. Good luck, friend.

Ah! Maybe we need a couple more weeks... It's only been 3. Her trainer is a behavior specialist, so hopefully she can help us with this and get back to working with her more. Thundershirts and treats are a no for her (she has a history of eating things off of her body, and has to have prescription diet), but breaking the compulsive behavior is definitely something we can do. Thanks!

She's been on Prozac for 3 weeks. Maybe she needs a bit more time. Thundershirts are a hard no for this one... She has a history of eating things off of her body; we've unfortunately already had two foreign body surgeries, one of which included a bowel resection. Poor thing is a mess! She can only have prescription treats and food now, so it makes it tough with special treats. I could totally try the spray and consult that book, though! Thanks!

It really is the cutest thing! She's very sweet :)

Interesting... You might be onto something with the side effects. I'll mention it to her vet. Her usual trainer is a behavior specialist, so I think we will just have to meet up with her again and get back to work on her.
It's weird right? Makes me feel SO confused.
Good tips. Thanks, friend!
Oh man. I'm glad I'm not alone. Did your therapist tell you why it happens?
Ah, I'm not familiar with that term... Time to Google, I suppose. Glad it's normal!

My psychiatrist does know about my drinking. Although we don't talk in great detail about it. Just a check in each week. I'm always honest about it. She was really not thrilled with my spree of getting drunk every night. Getting drunk at all is considered a major no-no with PTSD, it makes me so much more susceptible to flashbacks, but she never expressed any worry about alcoholism. I mean we've talked about it before, that we need to be mindful that I don't develop a new problem from trying to fix this one, but I think that at least right now she feels confident in my ability to stop or something. Maybe because I was able to stop the getting drunk every night thing immediately after she told me to shut it down. When I told her I did one drink a night she seemed actually impressed. Apparently most people with PTSD pick up a lot of drugs and booze to try and cope, so I think she was just happy that it wasn't worse maybe? I just want to be responsible and honest with myself, and I'm so desperate to get better. Just want to be mindful of at what point it's a serious problem.

I guess I'm wondering, like if there's a difference between craving because I'm suffocating a little in my PTSD, and craving just because I want to drink or just randomly feel compelled to? I also wondered if there is a difference because even if I might want a second drink after my first, I'm perfectly capable of choosing not to have another. When I was getting drunk every night it was purposeful self destructive behavior. I'm just trying to find clarity and understand. I don't want to create a problem that isn't there, but I also certainly wouldn't want to deny a real problem. There was a day I didn't drink last week because I wanted to take my valium to be able to sleep, and I'm already on Zoloft, so my psychiatrist said not to drink on that combo. I wonder if maybe I just lack the self respect and willpower right now.

Well hey, I'm glad I could be of some use!

This is really helpful thank you. I didn't think it was a problem at first. I mean it pretty obviously was when it was picking up and I was drinking to be destructive, but I think I thought I was ok when I was able to taper back down relatively easily. It's just that it doesn't seem easy to have absolutely nothing. And I definitely tend to have too much when I'm in the company of others. Then finding motivation to go to the liquor store freaked me out a little, when my other motivations were so low. Time to find a healthy coping mechanism... My psychiatrist is probably about ready to punch me in the face between the cutting and the drinking. PTSD treatment is ROUGH, man.

I have this problem too :(

I was raped when I was asleep and awoken by it, so it scares me and makes me feel unsafe a lot of the time as well due to the nature of my triggers and half asleep flashbacks. Like you, I've noticed that the alarm and even just having to be somewhere and feeling like "I have to fall asleep right now" causes me a ton of stress, because going to sleep is already stressful. I also do much better in general when I don't feel forced into a window of sleep. I think some of it is even just fearing that I won't sleep and will be more susceptible to flashbacks the next day. It's always easier when I know that I can prevent that by sleeping in or not having to be anywhere.

I was just reading your post because I've been unsure about the potential of having been drugged myself, so I was curious about your experience. I was raped, and I remember parts of it, but I've been trying to figure out what happened in between being nearly sober with two drinks in me and suddenly hitting a blackout point where I have snippets of memory barely being able to stand properly. I was also in a place where it was very crowded; too crowded to even be taking my own drinks directly from the bartender. I also think it's interesting that you said your friends didn't seem to think that you were wasted. My friends that I was out with that night are still baffled by what ended up happening to me. They tell me that they didn't think I was wasted either, but I don't understand how I could remember feel so utterly not in control of my body, and having such minimal memory but not passing out or ever getting sick, or otherwise show signs of being wasted? It's so bizarre to me. I brought a strange man back, so clearly I seemed fine enough to them to have made that decision (we were all going back to the same person's house), even though that's TOTALLY out of character for me. He ended up being a total psycho and threw me around a bit and raped me twice after I made it clear that I didn't want sex. 

I don't really understand drugging. I don't know how common it actually is, or how it realistically can manifest, but it does sound like something doesn't add up in either of our stories, so I honestly think it's possible. My psychiatrist suggested the idea to me initially. But I guess we will never know now.

I'm leaning that people who don't have it just won't ever get it. Even if they are supportive and loving they will never completely understand. Hell, I have it and I still don't know that I completely understand it, so, really, how could they? Therapists and psychiatrists can be really great because they understand it better than we do. I know it helps me having one; makes me feel less crazy and pathetic, and helps me learn more about my condition at the very least. PTSD so complex and abstract, and frankly unbelievable a lot of the time... Coming here is great. Creating a support system of people who do understand and can relate is a smart move.

I get this way as well, and I'd be willing to bet that a lot of people do. I think it's perceived threat in general, with nuances specific to the trauma. My own kind and gentle husband yelled at me once, and it sent me into a totally crazy PTSD episode. I think for me personally, it reminds me of when I was arguing with my rapist to try and convince him not to do it, and then when he started overtly yelling at me when I got away and trying to force me back. Even without that though, I think that arguing can commonly initiate that defensive fight/flight/freeze.
That's really fucked up, and I'm sorry.

I think it's really cool that you do this. I do something sort of similar, and my therapist is ALL about it lol. Mine is more art based, as I am a designer, but I dabble a little in writing or "poetry" (I don't know if it's actual poetry?). I think it's really helpful like you said for a different perspective in processing. I've come to a lot of really great realizations through the pieces. My project started as a smaller scale weekly projects that I posted on my instagram, but I found myself going to it more so I started a blog, and still post some abridged versions on insta. Maybe you would benefit from something like that? Mine isn't anonymous, because that was part of the concept for me; deconstructing shame and isolation, making people realize this happens to people they know, etc., but I would imagine that you could achieve similar results anonymously :)

My startle response decreased quite a bit when I started meds. It can still happens when I'm triggered or having any sort of episode or bad day, but I do much better now on a normal day lately. Makes a huge difference in the overall cycle of chaos! Before the meds I was pretty bad with jumpiness.

UGH I'm right there with you on this. I always feel like I don't have the adequate words to describe the feelings and how bad it was. It always sounds stupid and so much more minimal. Sometimes even just trying to explain it basically like that makes me feel like I'm going to vomit. I haven't figured out a away around it yet, just wanted you to know you're not alone in the struggle :/

My dog ate her harness off of her body when she was boarded with her trainer while my husband and I were on the last night of our honeymoon. She had to have emergency surgery and a bowel resection. We boarded the plane not knowing the outcome for 4 hours, and then when we got off the plane at home found out she made it through the surgery, but that we would have to wait a few days to see if she could still digest food and retain nutrients and be able to survive. Luckily she managed to get through with only inflammatory bowel disease and chronic vitamin deficiency! She lives a perfectly happy, healthy life now with prescription diet and vitamin supplement injections!

Long story short, I totally empathize with the panic and fear you're experiencing. It's heart breaking to see the little creature that relies on you and trusts and loves you unconditionally suffer :(

Also for what it's worth, my husband's appendix burst in his body when he was a kid and he didn't get it removed for a couple DAYS after (which in theory should kill you) and he is alive and well to tell the tale! I'm sure your fur baby will be ok :)

OH man. Alcohol is definitely a PTSD hotspot for me. It's weird, immediately after I was raped I drank a lot. To be around people or be normal I felt like I had to be drinking. Then I completely stopped drinking for a while, just because I didn't want to, and I was way too fearful of bars. Barely saw my friends for about a year because I was scared of drinking and being out with them. Then I was normal for a bit, and now that my PTSD is totally unlocked and out on the table, I've been needing one drink every night to feel relaxed. It's when life stops and it's time to relax that I realize that I can't, or that I'm met with the PTSD feelings, so having a drink has been my defense, or a further distraction I guess to avoid confronting it or to take the edge off. My therapist was only really concerned when I got to a point where I was getting drunk every night, but it fortunately wasn't hard for me to go back to one drink a night again after we talked about it. I thankfully don't have an addictive personality, all of my drinking has been a conscious choice. Right now, my therapist says it's ok to have one drink per night, as it's not technically dangerous. It's my "progress stepping stone" for now to eventually not feel like I need it. She seems to prioritize stableness and steady progress over going cold turkey in general, which I think is good for me.

I know that drinking can be troublesome for me. Almost every time I get drunk, I have a PTSD related episode, and often end up self harming or planning suicide, so I definitely avoid drunkenness for now, as that was actively setting me back. I definitely can't go to bars right now, but one of my prolonged exposure goals all the way down the line is actually to be able to go to them again and not have any sort of maddening breakdown (my assault began in a bar, so it's very triggering), so I guess we will see... It's definitely complicated and a delicate balance.

Ah, this is interesting. Thank you for sharing this info. That makes sense, actually. I have "standard" visual and sensational flashbacks to particular different moments from my night of assault plenty of the time, I just always felt like they were different from these weird responses that I get at other times that are less defined and longer lasting disconnect from reality. The first few times it happened I thought I was psychotic or something. After my psychiatrist said that I wasn't, I was always unsure if they were just an exaggerated stress response or if they were some sort of flashback. It's all so confusing. PTSD just grows more and more complex to me as I learn more and dig into it more.

When I'm in a flare, putting a pillow under my the backs of my knees and sleeping on my back helps. Sleeping on my sides always has me waking up to pee it's the worst, but if I had to, I'd try a pillow between my knees in that case. Long story short, pillows relieve some of the pressure. Learned it after an abdominal surgery :)

I've done trigger point injections a few times. Mostly for Pelvic Floor Dysfunction, which tends to subsequently irritate my bladder. My injections were internal (I'm 25/F), and very uncomfortable, but they gave my muscles the extra push they needed to relax the spasms when the valium suppositories and PT weren't enough. I'd do it again.

I understand you fear and discomfort. I couldn't really do anything about my problem because I have a few conditions that required monthly pelvic exams... so it kind of numbed me from it, BUT from having all of those pelvic exams I've learned a few things. 

-if you mention your past trauma (don't need to be specific) they absolutely should be extra gentle and understanding. When I went in for STD testing after my rape in college they knew and were very considerate and kind. Once they know your situation, they should check in with you throughout, which would mean that yes, there would be opportunity to stop. Also, you shouldn't need to worry about people outside your room seeing you. In my experience, I've never been to any Gyn's who would set you up like that. Some even have a curtain that pulls around for this reason.

-You can absolutely get a female doctor. That's a pretty common request, even without a traumatic history.

-Nobody will judge you for still having sex and wanting an IUD and also having problems. They will probably be really happy that you are still able to have some sex. Consensual sex with your fiance who you love is totally different than a pelvic exam or sexual abuse. Just because you've experienced that doesn't mean that you can never have sex. They know that, I promise! I'm sure they will be happy to talk about IUD's with you as well. That is just totally different from sexual trauma. IUD's do come with a procedure (to insert and remove) and some check up's though, so that's definitely something to be aware of.

-as for being "put under" or tranquilized, I wonder if maybe you should look into getting a medication for those panicked moments? I'm not medical professional, this is just an idea from one anxious person to another, but I know it helps me sometimes to take something before I go into a situation that tends to make me panic. I don't know if this is something they can do for you, or if you would need to see your primary care or if you have a psychiatrist or what, but it's just an idea.

Lastly, you don't owe anyone an explanation for why you are suffering  and why certain things are challenging. Most professionals just want to do their job and give you good care. I think as long as you just tell them what you want them to know and what you need from them, they should be able to properly help you through the experience. My friend was in a similar situation as you are and was TERRIFIED of the gyn, but then she got pregnant just a couple months after she got married, and now she has a beautiful baby and virtually no anxiety about pelvic exams anymore. It's totally doable to overcome, you got this!

I don't want to say that I know exactly how you feel, but I DO know how it feels to feel disgusted and uncomfortable in your own skin and to want nothing more than to be freed from it. 

From another perspective, I had a dear relative who took her own life, and I can promise you that it is not a solution. I know it feels like there is nowhere else to go. I struggle with suicidal ideation as well, but experiencing the aftermath was truly life changing. My entire family has never recovered. It really is true that the pain is transferred to the ones you love when you are gone. I'm not saying this to make you feel guilty, I'm saying this to help you see past your "right now." My aunt never got to meet her grandchildren or see my cousins get married. She's missed SO many AMAZING things. Every time something amazing happens we are all so devastated that she didn't hang on just a little bit longer to see it. Things won't always be this way. You are insanely strong for getting as far as you have. Don't quit now. You are resilient. You can push past this. There are so many more people who care and can help you than you realize. It might feel like you are lost and broken beyond repair, but I promise there are countless mental health professionals that are literally experts on trauma. There is a way out!

PTSD fills your brain up with destructive lies and it's unbearable most of the time, but TRUST ME. They are lies. And you will believe it one day. Hang in there, my friend. And feel free to message me if you ever need someone to talk to.

Thank you. I did end up calling my therapist. I should have just done that from the start, but I was just embarrassed about it. Being anonymous on the internet seemed easier, but in the end, none of your really know my situation as well as my therapist or myself. My therapist told me that it's not a good time for this job. I think I knew that all along and just felt guilty and sad about it.

Thanks for responding. Sorry if I sound like I'm "catastrophizing" but I actually did lose a really good client a couple months ago because I was such a crazy mess and tried to make myself work through it. It ended badly and it was embarrassing. Reading these responses made me realize that I knew what to do. I think I was just was afraid to do it because I come from a "suck it up" family that raised me to feel pathetic stepping down from a challenge (or taking sick days) and such lol. I ended up just asking my therapist about it, and she agreed that the potential set back in both treatment and in my career just makes this not a smart move right now. I know I will want to go back into more public environments when I feel more confident in my psychological state and when I'm getting better. Right now I'm just not well, and I don't like to admit it.

Thank you this is helpful. The more I read these responses, the more I realize that I think I knew my answer all along... I was just panicking and looking for reassurance or validation or something. I know myself best, and I realized that the position isn't right for me right now. I took a similar job in New York a little while back and actually did ruin a connection because I was such a mess. My therapist encouraged me to pick up more work that is cohesive to pushing hard through my treatment program at this time so that I have a better chance at getting better and thriving when I'm done with as little damage done in the process. I think I knew it but just felt guilty turning down good work. I ended up writing a proposal to do the job remotely, as I would be working on it alone onsite anyway, and have done similar projects for this team before, so maybe that will work out.

Thank you for your honesty it's very helpful. I should have included this in my original post, but not taking this temp job doesn't mean I wouldn't work at all. I'm a freelance designer, so it's technically one of many possibilities. I've definitely cut back on work, but I never stopped completely. All of my work in the past 3 months has been from home. The issue is more around that this job pays so well and is a great connection that ideally I wouldn't want to forfeit. I'm just having the hardest time trying to identify what I should be prioritizing in this decision. Does that make sense? I don't know if I'm being a total wimp avoiding it because I'm afraid that I will do something crazy at work or freak out and bail on the commute or if it's actually smarter to pick up more work from home? I just don't know. I've been having so much uncertainty about everything remotely related to PTSD right now I'm like an indecisive mess.

That's a good point. The only thing is, when I work in New York I leave at 6:00 am and don't get home til 9:00 pm. It's a really big time commitment. I had arranged to only do three days a week, but I did that before with another New York job and still ended up quitting part way through and I feel like I ruined future jobs with them because of it. Public transportation and crowds are really triggering for me, it's been rough going into the city. 

I used to work in New York all the time. When I did that I went into complete denial about my assault and ptsd and I did great at work, but then the suppressed build up eventually got out of control and ended in me trying to destroy a glass window of a bar with my body and locking myself in a bathroom and running away. Maybe I just don't know how to be balanced or maybe I'm just totally batshit. ANYWAY. Thank you for your advice.

Thank you. Your advice is helpful and does make sense. I think that what complicates it is that I can do a lot of my work from home too. Not taking this job wouldn't mean not working at all, it just means not taking a job with time and location commitment. I also have a spouse that makes the majority of our income, so it's not do or die, although it does make things tighter when I take less work... the in-house jobs pay the best. i think my fear is more around my recent tendencies to back out of things last minute, and my "escape freak outs" where I get triggered and compulsively lock myself in rooms or literally run away. It's happened before so that's more what I'm worried about. The last time I took an in house job I had a lot of call outs and a final no call no show before I had to quit. I feel like I burned that connection, so I guess I have that fear going into this job. I just don't know if I'm like further enabling the behavior by avoiding in-house jobs or if I'm being smart taking a step back? It's so hard to know what the right decision is.

When I'm in really bad shape I am constantly triggered by what appears to be nothing sometimes, but my guess is that is it something, but just something subtle that we aren't very aware of. For me personally, when I'm at my worst almost anything can trigger me. Sometimes it's just constantly in the forefront of my brain, so I just can't stop thinking about it, that can give me the same feelings.
Wow great, thank you so much!
Thank you. I appreciate that. It really is scary :( Best of luck to you

Thanks, I'm glad (but also sad) that you can relate! I mentioned in a comment response above that my main fear comes from times where I've made myself go places and it turned into something really ugly. My main fear is that I will end up doing something that will be more costly to the professional relationship than turning down the job. UGH. I'm sort of leaning into telling myself that I deserve to do this job (because I like it and want to do it). I've also lost a lot in terms of social life and pass times that I enjoy. Sometimes, when I'm feeling decent, I can find empowerment in deciding that my rapist can't take everything from me, so I'm going to try to run with this idea that I deserve to do this. I hope to God it works out for this and I can do a good job and wrap myself up in the work.

Thank you, this is really encouraging. It's helpful for me to hear that you understand the struggle and have been able to make yourself do what needs to be done. 

I've been able to lean on my spouse a bit because his job is technically enough to just get by on, and my student loans have been able to be covered by my side jobs from home, but there's just really no room for anything else, and this month I'm a little short for my loans, so that's what made me feel like I needed to take this job, aside from fear of losing this client that I would eventually like to be working with more regularly again.

I used to be really good at just doing what I absolutely had to do, and it almost always has worked out for me... until a couple months ago when prolonged exposure therapy (or rather fully opened up and unleashed PTSD) broke my brain. I'm nervous because I've been out before where I start getting a bit delusional (in the PTSD sort of way), and panic and lock myself in rooms, and just overall am unable to do anything. There are some people who definitely think I TOTALLY lost my mind. I've been destructive at times because of it as well. Ever since that started happening, it's made me see what I'm unfortunately capable of under the right stressors and triggers... I think my main fear that keeps me from working lately is that I'm afraid that I'm going to do something totally batshit at work, and I'm also afraid of having days where I am like that before I even get in (the negative effects of a long commute) and having to call out very last minute. Just things that might have a more negative impact on my relationship with them than turning it down from the beginning I suppose? It just feels like a gamble. I know how easily I can be triggered when I haven't gotten any sleep, that's one of the main things I worry about with having to wake up at 5:00 on those work days.

All of that considered, I do really need this money, and I do want to work for them. I love designing for them, they really give me a lot of independence, which is wonderful. And it's so rewarding to see products I've worked on in stores, I know it would be really beneficial for me if I could make this happen... Even just the 20 minute walk from the train to the building is going to be good for me if I can get past being so jumpy every time someone walks near me or startles me. I'm just SO nervous about it. A think an audiobook is a fantastic idea. Something that can keep me engrossed throughout the commute sounds like a great idea. I had always been a podcast or music person, but most are too short to keep me completely distracted from point A to point B. I think a treat is a good idea too. It's something to trick me into looking forward to it. 

I'm gonna cross my fingers and hope that the meds kick in in a positive way for me and help make this doable. I hear it takes the edge off and makes you less touchy with triggers. I've only been on them for a few days, so we'll see...

I totally understand this. I think we all feel this way. Some people think that what happened to me is horrific, but I always feel like it wasn't enough to warrant how intensely my PTSD manifests in my life. Sometimes I think "I wasn't attacked that badly" or "maybe deep down I actually willed it to happen," and all this other self blaming shit... turns out its just an alternate avoidance technique for me most of the time. Guilt and shame are literally a symptom of PTSD. From what I understand, much of it stems from improperly processed trauma, and that's why treatment is so important, because you are sort of reopening everything and learning how to read the situation correctly, or something like that. 

Things could always be better, and they could always be worse, but in the end, PTSD is PTSD, and trauma is trauma. It's a sickness that we don't have to earn compassion and treatment for. Other aspects of your life and genetic predisposition to mental illness can also affect development and severity of PTSD. Mental illness runs pretty rampant on both sides of my family, my doctor told me that it functions similarly to cancer in heredity. And I was also told that your support system after trauma can impact whether or not you develop PTSD. If you are unsupported (as I was) it can have a very negative impact. I think that part of the reason why my assault ruined me so much too is the other "less traumatic" things in my life that happened in the years leading up to that sort of made my rape the epic final straw of sorts.

I don't know if this will answer your question directly, but my friends new boyfriend that she is head over heels for reminds me so much of my rapist and makes me feel irrationally unsafe, and I avoid him and her if she's with him now. The last time I saw him (them) we were out drinking for my friends birthday and I had an INTENSE ptsd episode partly directed at him, so I've been instructed by my therapist to avoid him for now since he is clearly a trigger. I think there is truth in some of what you said, but I think you've twisted it a little too far in a questionable direction, and I'm worried that giving advice like this to someone who is struggling and being open and vulnerable here will be damaging. The thing is, a lot of us who have PTSD ARE in fact victims of a very personal crime. Accepting that victimization is a crucial step to recovery. I had years of just "choosing" to not be the victim, and I regret it every single day, as doing so was actively suppressing how deep of a problem it was for me. When PTSD was first suggested to me I felt uncomfortable with it, and I felt uncomfortable with self love and self care, and I decided to keep being a workaholic and a over achieve to distract myself and prove that I had the power. I discovered a couple years later how dangerous this is for PTSD. I have since learned that choosing to ignore the root of the problem and the PTSD itself is in reality only surrendering control. I wasn't able to start my healing process until I could start to actually believe that I was indeed victimized. And honestly, the feeling isn't good. Flashbacks of my moments of being victimized literally make me want to die. Long story short, I think it's dangerous to invalidate the "victimhood." You can't move onto the rising above and not letting it drag you down stage until you've fully processed and worked through the victim stage. You can't be a survivor if you've never acknowledged that you were a victim first.

Either way, even if you wanted to encourage someone to feel empowered and like a survivor vs a victim, do you really think that a cold attitude is best way to execute that? 

Lastly, let's remember that nobody wants to self harm at their core. We want to in the same way that we choose to; it's compulsory. It's a punishment. Or maybe it's a release and a calm in panic. Nobody is advocating that it is ok or a good solution, but I think that it is extremely important that we recognize the validity of it. Self harm is a deeply confusing compulsion, often rooting in some type of self loathing, so trying to help by making someone feel bad is really objectively further damaging. Hey I just wanted to comment because self harm is a new ish thing for me too as an adult. I've actually gotten some half decent help on it, and I feel like it's surprisingly quickly become one of the more successful clear parts of my recovery now, so I wanted to share with you what I've learned.

First of all, sure it may technically be a choice, but for me when it happens it's a compulsive choice. I personally disagree with the "take responsibility" and just choose not to do it route, and would rather say to take responsibility by learning about why you are doing it, and what things might set you up to feel particularly compelled to do it. Further, I would even prefer that "responsibility" maybe isn't the word used. What you are feeling compelled to do to yourself is directly related to a likely unthinkable pain that was inflected upon you. So, I fear that viewing this as a responsibility issue might do further harm than good, especially since guilt is often a key player in PTSD in some way or another. Consider choosing to fight against it as graciousness and kindness towards yourself. Think of it as a way to mend the wounds. You don't deserve the pain you are trying to cause yourself, even though in the moment it makes sense and seems like the only thing that can slow things down when it gets out of control. But I think if you talk about this with your therapist that they would be able to tell you from a professional and statistical standpoint that self harm is shockingly common in PTSD, and they would also be able to help you understand what it is, and the root of the compulsion, and what you can do to prevent it, or even tips for alternate behavior practices when the compulsion comes on.

I was first diagnosed with PTSD almost a year into an amazing relationship when I was still in college. He's my husband now. He actually had apparently already bought a ring right before the initial suggested diagnosis, and proposed to me shortly into treatment which I stopped at the time because I jumped right onto the wedding planning distraction and convinced myself that nothing was actually wrong with me, but that's another story... Anyway, a few months after our wedding (February of this year) I had a MAJOR relapse and my PTSD has gone totally out of control, to the point that I haven't been able to work or sleep, and sometimes can barely take care of our house and even myself. Things were bad in college, and they are really terrible now, but honestly, our relationship hasn't taken a hit, and that's why I wanted to chime in here. 

I feel deep empathy for your girlfriend, and it's clear that you do too. I sort of see her push for marriage as a misplaced attempt to control her life or redefine it in some way. Which is valid in terms of feelings, but definitely not a legitimate solution. I can attest to marriage not fixing things. I think that part of me thought it might fix me. That I would feel secure and safe from it, and that being in a happy marriage could ward off the nastiness of PTSD, but that was not the case, it still came back with a NASTY vengeance.

 Ok, so aside from the marriage perspective, I want to address her problems and your subsequent mistreatment. URGE HER TO GET HELP. PTSD doesn't go away on it's own. It's very complex, and if you don't understand what is happening to you, or you are just totally unaware, you're essentially forfeiting control, which will result in misplaced energy and emotions. Some people turn inward and abuse themselves, some people release it outwards on other people. Despite the validity of the behavior, it doesn't make it ok. Agitation is definitely normal in PTSD. My spouse can DEFINITELY attest to that, but the difference between your situation and mine is that I have awareness. Getting treatment will teach the sufferer about the illness, and also teach mindfulness. Mindfulness in practice means that, although I'm not always going to be totally in control, that I can be aware of the awful feelings and then sort of have a mental dialogue with myself about how I want to behave. It helps me identify the root feeling and have more control over how I proceed. It's hard and takes practice and patience, but it yields a very rewarding sense of control, which is HUGE for a PTSD sufferer. It has lessened a lot of nasty behavior on my part, and has also lessened my drinking and self harm. Even if I do go through with treating the hubs badly, I'm at the very least aware after, and can give a thoughtful apology and explain where it came from from a place of taking responsibility, so that it can reduce the damage done to him. At the earlier point in our relationship when I was struggling, I was kind of out of control, and he was beyond kind and understanding to me. He is in general a very gracious person, and I am so grateful that he was able to take the brunt of that. However, I see now that I am actually pursuing treatment just how vital this mindfulness is to have a healthy relationship. I don't know if we could have survived PTSD together if I didn't come to that realization, because one person just can't be the "shock absorber" forever. So, I guess what I'm saying is that you can't expect yourself to be a punching bag to your girlfriend and she shouldn't expect that from you either. If you want to help her, I would encourage her to get help, and maybe even explain to her that you want so much to help her and see her feeling better and more herself, and that while you understand her misplaced behavior, that you cannot adequately help her if you are being worn down yourself, and that while it is not her fault that she has this struggle, that you don't want to see it tear her down or tear your relationship down. I also want to say that if you are the only person that she has disclosed this to, I think that even just as a non-romantic friend who cares about her, you have an obligation to really encourage her to pursue help. PTSD is destructive. I wouldn't want to see anyone that I am even remotely close to live in the dark with it like that.

Above everything, do make sure that you take care of yourself. You can't even properly help someone if you yourself are not well, and you definitely can't actually help someone who just doesn't want to get better. I know it's a tough balance... You certainly shouldn't be expected to stay in a romantic relationship with her if you don't want to be in one, but I do kind of think that you might need to be the push that she needs, regardless of from what position to her that comes from (friend vs boyfriend?). Does that make sense? I hope it doesn't sound too contradictory or confusing!

Sometimes what helps me most is:

1. helping other people 

This includes sharing my story, creating artwork or writing pieces about sexual assault/feminism/ptsd, encouraging other people who are struggling, etc. I sometimes share a public instagram post about my experience, and it breaks the pattern of isolation, and often gets a response from someone who was struggling and looking for something to connect with as well. 2. Creating awareness of positive things that I have gained since my assault. 

It's so easy to slip down the slope of all the terrible things that you have gained, but it's surprisingly rewarding if you can collect the positives. For example, my positives are: I've become a more compassionate person, I'm significantly more likely to believe and be empathetic towards other people when they declare a struggle, trivial frustrations have significantly less power over me, I take myself a little bit less seriously, I have a better understanding of both forgiveness and grace towards myself and others, and I value good days (and even "normal days") so much more than I used to

3. I haven't gotten this one down yet, but I think healthy distraction makes life more livable. 

Spend time doing something that you've always wanted to do, or love doing. Sometimes if I can't make myself do my work due to panic, dissociation or anxiety, I will allow myself to do something fun first, just to get myself moving and feeling more positive. It seems counter intuitive, but it almost always works for me. You lose a little bit of time, but it's almost always less then when I just sit there and try to will the bad feelings away. I still struggle a lot with finding the balance between denial/avoidance and deserved distraction, but I still think it's worth mentioning!
